paras: The horsewhipping of Frank Allen was an attack on a Black man from Gainesville, Georgia, who was whipped at gunpoint by two white men at Demorest, Georgia, in early February 1903 and then driven out of town. The attackers, C. L. Adams and Edgar Taylor, were said to be avenging an insult Allen had allegedly offered their orphan niece months before. The episode reached print as a short wire item in two Georgia dailies, which gave only the attackers' grievance.

Several months before the attack, Allen had worked in a livery stable at Demorest. According to the dispatch, he met an orphan niece of Adams and Taylor on the street one day and "made very offensive remarks to her, which sent her home crying at the insult." The same report added that "he would have been more severely dealt with had he not been spirited away" at that time.

On a Wednesday morning, which by the calendar was February 4, 1903, Adams and Taylor attacked Allen at Demorest. Taylor held him up with a revolver while Adams "laid on a heavy whip with great vigor." After the whipping, which both papers called severe, Allen was driven out of town.
No report of an arrest, charge or other legal action against Adams or Taylor was found, and the coverage contains no statement from Allen.

The Americus Times-Recorder printed the item first, on February 6, under the headline "Used Lash on Negro" and the subhead "Charged with Insulting Young Lady at Demorest, Ga." Its dateline misprinted the town as "Demorest, Pa.," and it described Allen as "a yellow negro from Gainesville." The Savannah Morning News ran nearly the same text a day later on an inside page under "Negro Horsewhipped," but its column broke off mid-sentence before the account of the insult was finished.

Both papers told the story from the attackers' side, presenting the alleged remark to the girl as "the cause of the trouble" and the whipping without comment. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Horsewhipping of Frank Allen
bases: Two named white men whipped one Black man at gunpoint and drove him out of town over an alleged insult; no band, night riding or warning notice is reported, so the record's 'whitecapping' is not supported (A1, A2).
Both reports are the same wire text, nearly word for word, so they are one account rather than independent corroboration (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Wire report (attackers' side)
accounts.gist: Adams and Taylor whipped Allen at gunpoint and drove him out of town because, months earlier, he had allegedly insulted their orphan niece on the street; he had escaped worse treatment then only by being 'spirited away'.

framing.detail: Both Georgia papers ran the same brief; the Americus headline 'Used Lash on Negro' and subhead 'Charged with Insulting Young Lady' put the accusation forward, and neither paper questioned the whipping or reported Allen's side.

conflicts.note: The 'Pa.' dateline is a typesetting error: the same item's headline gives Demorest, Ga., and both papers place Allen's home in Gainesville.
